title: Michael Ventris and the decoding of Linear B

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The urge to discover secrets is deeply ingrained in human nature; even the least curious mind is aroused by the promise of sharing knowledge that others do not have access to. Few people are fortunate enough to find a job which consists of the solution of mysteries, whether it be the physicist who tracks down a hitherto unknown nuclear particle or the policeman who finds a criminal. But most of us are driven to satisfy this urge by the solving of artificial puzzles devised for our entertainment. Detective stories or crossword puzzles cater for the majority; the solution of secret codes may be the hobby of a few. This is the story of the solving of a genuine mystery which had puzzled experts for half a century.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In 1936 a 14-year-old schoolboy was among a group who visited Burlington House in London, to see an exhibition organised to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the British School of Archaeology at Athens. They heard a lecture by a very famous old archaeologist, Sir Arthur Evans, who told them of his discovery of a long forgotten civilisation on the Greek island of Crete, and of the mysterious writing used by the prehistoric people who had lived there. In that hour a seed was planted that was to bear dramatic fruit 16 years later, for one of the boys who attended the lecture was already keenly interested in ancient scripts and languages. At the age of seven he had bought and studied a German book on the ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs. After the lecture he vowed to take up the challenge of the Cretan writing, which became generally known as Minoan, named after the ancient Cretan king, Minos. It was also called Linear B. The boy began to read the books already published on the script, and even started a correspondence with the people who were closely involved in researching it. In the fullness of time he was to succeed where they had failed. His name was Michael Ventris.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Michael had been born in 1922 to a well-to-do family with an English father and a Polish mother, and began his education in Switzerland, where he developed his love of learning. He mastered French, German, Swiss-German and Swedish. Back in England he studied the classics (Latin and Greek), but did not attend university.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ventris studied architecture at the Architectural Association School in London, and joined the Royal Air Force during World War II. After the war he worked as an architect for a time with a team at the Ministry of Education engaged in the design of new schools, and in 1956, because of the quality of his work, he was awarded a research fellowship. He may well have become one of the leading figures in his profession; but it was not in this way that he was to win fame. He never lost his interest in the Minoan script, and with a rare concentration, devoted most of his spare time to painstaking studies of the difficult problem of understanding it. In 1952 he claimed to have found the key to its understanding, and to have proved that the language written in the Minoan script was an early form of Greek. From the beginning he advanced his claims with suitable caution and hesitancy, a promising sign to those who had repeatedly experienced the assurance of previous colleagues. His claims were fully vindicated in subsequent years, but even when his success was assured he remained simple and unassuming.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: ‘Those whom the gods love die young,’ said the Greek poet Menander. And so it was with Ventris. No-one dreamed that the life which had shown so much genius and held promise of so much more would be cut short in the very hour of triumph. In September 1956, while driving home, Ventris’s car was hit by a lorry and he was killed instantly. He was just 34 years old.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If we ask what were the special qualities which made his achievement possible, we can point to his capacity for infinite care, his powers of concentration, and his meticulous accuracy. The Minoans were to him no vague abstractions, but a living people whose thoughts he could penetrate. He laid stress on the visual approach to the texts, and made himself so familiar with them that large sections were imprinted on his mind simply as patterns, long before the decipherment gave them meaning. But a photographic memory was not enough, and it was here that his architectural training came to his aid. The architect’s eye looks beneath the appearance of the building and distinguishes the significant parts of the pattern, the structural elements and framework of the building. So Ventris was able to discern, among the bewildering variety of the mysterious signs, patterns and regularities which betrayed the underlying structure. It is this quality, the power to see order in apparent confusion, which has marked the work of all great men.

subtitle: Linear B is the name of an ancient script, discovered on the island of Crete in the Mediterranean Sea. Michael Ventris, an English scholar, was the first person to discover how to read inscriptions written in that alphabet
